question.prompt:
Of the following

\((1)\quad a(x-y)=ax-ay\)

\((2)\quad a^{x-y}=a^x-a^y\)

\((3)\quad \log(x-y)=\log x-\log y\)

\((4)\quad \dfrac{\log x}{\log y}=\log x-\log y\)

\((5)\quad a(xy)=ax\times ay\)

solutions.explanation:
Here a statement is understood to be true if it holds for every choice of variables for which its expressions are defined. One allowed counterexample disproves such a claim.

Statement (1) is the distributive law:
\[
a(x-y)=ax-ay.
\]

For statement (2), take \(a=2\), \(x=3\), and \(y=1\). Its two sides are
\[
2^{3-1}=4,
\qquad 2^3-2^1=6,
\]
so it is false in general.

For the logarithms, use any fixed base \(b>0\), \(b\ne1\). In statement (3), take \(x=2\) and \(y=1\). The left side is \(\log 1=0\), while the right side is \(\log 2\ne0\), since \(b^0=1\ne2\).

In statement (4), take \(x=y=2\). Because \(\log 2\ne0\), the quotient is defined and equals \(1\), while the difference equals \(0\).

In statement (5), take \(a=2\) and \(x=y=1\). Then \(a(xy)=2\), whereas \(ax\times ay=2\times2=4\).

Thus only statement (1) is an identity, giving choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Prove the identity and test the others
